questions.q: Find the total number of prime factors in the expression $30^{15} \times 22^{11} \times 15^{24}$.
questions.s:
Final Output: $115$

Pen-Free Observation: Options sab $110+$ hain. Prime factor sum base splitting par depend karega.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Dekh bhai, sidha bases ko primes me tod: $30=2\times3\times5$ (3 primes), $22=2\times11$ (2 primes), $15=3\times5$ (2 primes). Total sum = $3(15) + 2(11) + 2(24) = 45 + 22 + 48 = 115$. Khatam.

Takeaway: 'Total prime factors' bole to individual primes ki powers ka sum karte hain, distinct nahi.

questions.q: What are the last two digits of $4^{4^4}$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $96$

Pen-Free Observation: Power tower with base $4$. Result will definitely be even, ruling out odd trap logic.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): $4^{256} = 2^{512}$. Initial logic validated. Leap directly to transformation: $2^{12} \times (2^{10})^{50} = 4096 \times (1024)^{\text{Even}}$. Modulo $100$ extraction gives $96 \times 76 \equiv 96$.

Takeaway: Any number ending in $76$ multiplied by $X$ retains the last two digits of $X$ (if $X$ is a power of $2$).

Final Output: $9$

Pen-Free Observation: Factorial $>4!$ ends in $0$, to aage check hi nahi karna. Just evaluate $1!$ to $4!$.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Standard processing applied for $1!$ to $3!$ giving unit sum $1+6+6=13$. Leap to $4!$: Base $24$, Power is even. $4^{\text{Even}}$ ends in $6$. Total unit sum $13+6 = 19 \implies 9$.

Takeaway: SSC CGL trap! Factorial powers ko jaldi evaluate karo. $4^{\text{Even}}$ hamesha $6$ deta hai.

questions.q: Find the total number of factors of $(73^3 - 40^3 - 33^3)$.
questions.s:
Final Output: $192$

Pen-Free Observation: $a+b+c = 73-40-33 = 0$. Identity alert!

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): $a^3+b^3+c^3 = 3abc$. Transformation: $3 \times 73 \times 40 \times 33 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5^1 \times 11^1 \times 73^1$. Exponents jump: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 192$.

Takeaway: Algebra aur Number System ka deadly combo. Sum of bases zero ho to direct $3abc$ me tod do.

questions.q: If a 9-digit number $897359y7x$ is divisible by $72$, then what is the value of $(3x + 4y)$ for the largest possible value of $y$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $54$

Pen-Free Observation: Divisibility by $72$ means check $8$ and $9$. Target is 'largest' $y$.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Assume max $y=9$. Last 3 digits $97x / 8 \implies x=6$. Digital sum for $9$: $48 + x + y = 48+6+9 = 63$ (Divisible). Set $y=9, x=6$. Final equation: $18+36=54$.

Takeaway: Largest/smallest word par dhyan de bhai, CGL yahi fasaega.

questions.q: Find the number of proper divisors of $3^6 \times 5^4$.
questions.s:
Final Output: $34$

Pen-Free Observation: 'Proper' divisors pucha hai, total nahi. Formula is Total Factors - $1$.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Powers me $+1$ karke multiply kar: $7 \times 5 = 35$. Proper hone ke chakkar me $1$ minus kar de: $34$.

Takeaway: Proper divisors me original number ko count nahi karte.

questions.q: If the 8-digit number $8439x53y$ is divisible by $99$, then what is the value of $(x^2 + y^2)$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $16$

Pen-Free Observation: Divisibility by $99$ means applying $11$ and $9$ rules simultaneously.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): $11$ rule leap: $x-y = 4$. $9$ rule leap: $32+x+y \equiv 0 \pmod 9 \implies x+y = 4$. Simultaneous solve gives $x=4, y=0$. Result $4^2+0^2 = 16$.

Takeaway: Variables set karte time check kar liya kar bhai ki digit $0-9$ ke bahar na jaye.

questions.q: Let $y$ be the least number which is divisible by $22, 33, 36$, and $66$, and is also a perfect cube. Find the sum of the digits of the remainder when $y$ is divided by $179$.
questions.s:
Final Output: $4$

Pen-Free Observation: Perfect cube aur LCM ka mix. Multipliers missing honge.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): LCM $= 396 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 11$. Cube completion needs $2^1 \times 3^1 \times 11^2 = 726$. Number $y = 396 \times 726 = 287496$. Leap to division: $287496 \pmod{179} = 22$. Digits sum $= 4$.

Takeaway: Cube/Square banane ke liye factors ki power ko $3$ ya $2$ ke multiple tak push karte hain.

questions.q: If $N = 4^{11} + 4^{12} + 4^{13} + 4^{14}$, then find the total number of positive factors of $N$.
questions.s:
Final Output: $92$

Pen-Free Observation: Series of powers. Lowest power common niklegi.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Pull out $4^{11}$. Inside: $(1+4+16+64) = 85$. Prime rep: $2^{22} \times 5^1 \times 17^1$. Powers $+1$ multiplication: $23 \times 2 \times 2 = 92$.

Takeaway: Hamesha base ko absolute prime ($2, 3, 5$) me convert karna mat bhulna.

questions.q: What are the last two digits of $31^{41^{51}}$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $31$

Pen-Free Observation: Base ends in $1$. Aman Sir's universal rule for $X1$ applies.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Unit digit is always $1$. Tens digit = (Tens of base $\times$ Unit of power). $3 \times (\text{Last digit of } 41^{51})$. Since $41^{51}$ ends in $1$, $3 \times 1 = 3$. Answer: $31$.

Takeaway: $(\dots x1)^y$ ke last two digits hamesha $(x \times \text{last digit of } y)$ aur $1$ hote hain.

questions.q: How many composite numbers are there from $69$ to $91$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $18$

Pen-Free Observation: Small range. Total numbers me se prime hatane hain.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Total numbers $= 91-69+1 = 23$. Primes evaluated: $71, 73, 79, 83, 89$ (Total $5$). Composite $= 23 - 5 = 18$.

Takeaway: Range formula $= (L - F + 1)$ and directly skip prime traps.

questions.q: Remainder when $2025^{(2024^{3025})}$ is divided by $7$ is
questions.s:
Final Output: $4$

Pen-Free Observation: Euler's totient theorem will collapse the massive exponent.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Base transformation: $2025 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$. Totient of $7$ is $6$. Power transformation: $2024^{3025} \equiv 2^{\text{Odd}} \equiv 2 \pmod 6$. Final collapse: $2^2 \pmod 7 = 4$.

Takeaway: Fermat/Euler Totient is a cheat code for these massive power towers.

questions.q: If a book has $250$ pages, how many digits have been used to number the pages.
questions.s:
Final Output: $642$

Pen-Free Observation: $250$ pages standard pagination counting. $1$-digit, $2$-digit, $3$-digit slots.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): $1$ to $99$ takes exactly $189$ digits. Remaining $3$-digit pages $= 250 - 99 = 151$. Computation: $189 + (151 \times 3) = 642$.

Takeaway: Memorize: $1-99$ uses $189$ digits. $1-999$ uses $2889$ digits.

questions.q: What is the remainder when $15^{400}$ is divided by $1309$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $1$

Pen-Free Observation: $1309$ is a composite of $7 \times 11 \times 17$. Chinese Remainder Theorem logic.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Check mod $7, 11, 17$. $15^{400} \equiv 1$ across all three prime bases using Fermat's Little Theorem. Recombination gives $1 \pmod{1309}$.

Takeaway: Large weird divisors are always product of primes. Break them and conquer.

questions.q: Which of the following sets is a proper subset of rational numbers?
questions.s:
Final Output: Natural numbers

Pen-Free Observation: Pure number system hierarchy.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Natural $\subset$ Whole $\subset$ Integers $\subset$ Rationals $\subset$ Reals. Option validation complete. Natural numbers fit.

Takeaway: Diagrammatic clarity of number sets saves time.

questions.q: In how many ways can the number $11025$ be resolved into two factors which are co-prime to each other?
questions.s:
Final Output: $4$

Pen-Free Observation: Number of co-prime factor pairs strictly depends on the count of distinct prime bases.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Prime factorization of $11025 = 3^2 \times 5^2 \times 7^2$. Distinct bases $(n) = 3$. Jump to formula: $2^{n-1} = 2^2 = 4$.

Takeaway: Direct hack: Co-prime ways $= 2^{n-1}$ jaha $n$ = distinct prime factors.

questions.q: What is the value of $1006^2 - 1007 \times 1005 + 1008 \times 1004 - 1009 \times 1003$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $6$

Pen-Free Observation: Numbers are strictly consecutive around $1006$. Algebraic substitution is the key.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Let $x = 1006$. Pattern leap: $x^2 - (x^2-1) + (x^2-4) - (x^2-9) = 1 - 4 + 9 = 6$.

Takeaway: Never multiply! Treat consecutive massive numbers as $(x-a)(x+a)$ forms.

questions.q: What is the sum of the first $39$ odd numbers?
questions.s:
Final Output: $1521$

Pen-Free Observation: AP sum of odds starting from $1$ is just the square of the count.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Sum $= n^2 = 39^2 = 1521$.

Takeaway: First $n$ odd numbers sum $= n^2$. First $n$ even $= n(n+1)$.

questions.q: How many numbers between $200$ and $800$ are not divisible by $5$ and $7$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $411$

Pen-Free Observation: Range is exactly $600$. Divisibility exclusions follow a fractional depletion pattern.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Use consecutive block jump. Total $= 600$. Fraction remaining $= 600 \times (4/5) \times (6/7) \approx 411.4$. Round down to $411$.

Takeaway: Not divisible by $p, q$ over large uniform ranges is approximately Total $\times (1 - 1/p)(1 - 1/q)$.

questions.q: Find the last three digits of $2^{300}$.
questions.s:
Final Output: $376$

Pen-Free Observation: Last $3$ digits mean $\pmod{1000}$. Base $2$ and $1000$ share common factors. CRT is mandatory.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Split $1000 = 8 \times 125$. Mod $8$: $0$. Mod $125$: Euler jump $\implies 2^{100} \equiv 1 \implies 2^{300} \equiv 1$. Target is $125k + 1$ divisible by $8$. For $k=3$, $376$ fits perfectly.

Takeaway: Extreme level hack! CRT for non-coprime modulus is CDS/CGL Mains material.

questions.q: What is the ratio of the sum of the even factors to the sum of the odd factors of $240$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $30:1$

Pen-Free Observation: Ratio of even to odd factor sums isolates the base-$2$ component.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): $240 = 2^4 \times 3 \times 5$. Odd part sum $= (1+3)(1+5) = 24$. Even part sum removes $2^0$: $(2+4+8+16) \times 24 = 30 \times 24$. Ratio $= 30:1$.

Takeaway: Even factor sum me bas $2^0$ wala element ignore karna hota hai.

questions.q: What is the remainder when a 6-digit number formed by repeating a 2-digit number three times (for example, $252525$) is divided by $10101$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $0$

Pen-Free Observation: $ababab$ pattern itself is a multiple of $10101$.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): $ababab = ab(10101)$. Remainder when divided by $10101$ is inherently $0$.

Takeaway: Place value expansion patterns ($ab \to 101, abc \to 1001$) are instant visual solves.

questions.q: If $n = 8^{12}$, then how many perfect squares are there in its factors?
questions.s:
Final Output: $19$

Pen-Free Observation: Convert to prime base to trace all even exponents.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): $8^{12} = 2^{36}$. Perfect squares need even powers $\{0, 2, 4 \dots 36\}$. Count leap: $36/2 + 1 = 19$.

Takeaway: Total perfect squares $= (\text{Highest even power} / 2) + 1$ (for $0$).

questions.q: The 5-digit number $7x23y$ is divisible by $24$. Find the maximum possible value of $(x + y)$.
questions.s:
Final Output: $9$

Pen-Free Observation: Divisible by $24 \implies 8$ and $3$. Target is MAX $(x+y)$.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Rule of $8$ on $23y \implies y=2$. Rule of $3$ on sum: $14+x$. Max single digit $x$ for multiple of $3$ is $7$ (sum $21$). Hence $7+2=9$.

Takeaway: Divisibility me humesha pehle restrictive rule lagao (last digits), fir broad rule (sum).

questions.q: What is the remainder when the $7$-digit number $4538291$ is divided by $101$?
questions.s:
Final Output: $58$

Pen-Free Observation: Divisibility of $101$ works on $2$-digit alternating blocks from right.

Method 1 (Ninja Technique): Blocks: $04, 53, 82, 91$. Alternating sum: $91 - 82 + 53 - 04 = 58$. Remainder directly $58$.

Takeaway: Base $10^2+1$ (i.e. $101$) requires blocks of $2$. Base $10^3+1$ (i.e. $1001$) requires blocks of $3$.
